Apollyon
uh-POL-yuhn
proper noun
Greek Apollyon, the destroyer; the angel of the bottomless pit, called in Hebrew Abaddon (Rev 9:11).

📖 Biblical Definition

Apollyon is the name given in the Revelation to the angel of the bottomless pit—in Hebrew, Abaddon; in Greek, Apollyon—both meaning the Destroyer. And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon. The name reveals the character of Satan and his hosts: they are destroyers, whose work is ruin and death, for the devil was a murderer from the beginning, a thief who comes but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy. Apollyon is set in sharp contrast to Christ: the Destroyer against the Saviour, the one who kills against the one who gives life abundantly. In Bunyan’s great allegory, Apollyon meets Christian in the Valley of Humiliation and, straddling the whole breadth of the way, does battle with him; and Christian, sorely wounded, prevails at last by the sword of the Spirit and the blood of the Lamb, crying, Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. The dictionary honors the name Apollyon as a revelation of the destroying nature of the enemy of souls—not a harmless figure of folklore but a real and malignant destroyer—and as a summons to the believer’s warfare: that the Destroyer is met and overcome not by the strength of man but by Christ the Saviour, who came to destroy the works of the devil, and through whom His people are more than conquerors.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Destroyer, angel of the bottomless pit (Hebrew Abaddon); a name revealing Satan’s ruinous nature, overcome by Christ the Saviour and the blood of the Lamb.

APOLLYON, the Destroyer, angel of the bottomless pit (Rev 9:11).

In Hebrew Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon—both meaning Destroyer.

Reveals Satan’s nature: a murderer and destroyer from the beginning.

Set against Christ: the Destroyer versus the Saviour and Lifegiver.

📖 Key Scripture

Rev 9:11 — "And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon."

Joh 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

1Jo 3:8 — "He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil."

Rev 12:11 — "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Apollyon is dismissed as folklore or the devil denied altogether; Scripture reveals a real destroyer, overcome only by Christ and the blood of the Lamb.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of Apollyon as mere folklore, or the wider denial of the devil altogether—the comfortable modern unbelief that there is no personal adversary, no destroyer, no real spiritual enemy of the soul. But Scripture names him: the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name is Abaddon, Apollyon, the Destroyer (Rev 9:11); and the Lord Himself describes the thief who comes but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy (John 10:10). To deny the Destroyer is to disarm the believer before a real and malignant foe.

The principle to recover is the destroying nature of the enemy and the conquering work of Christ. Apollyon’s very name declares his work: ruin, death, destruction; he was a murderer from the beginning. But the Son of God was manifested for this purpose, that He might destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8)—the Saviour against the Destroyer, the Lifegiver against the murderer. And the saints overcome him not by their own strength but by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony, loving not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11). As Bunyan’s Christian prevailed over Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation, so the believer, sorely pressed, is yet more than conqueror through Him that loved him.
